title: A Split Decision: Supreme Court Shields Fed's Lisa Cook, But Hands Trump Broad Power Over Other Agencies
summary:
The Supreme Court handed down two landmark decisions on Thursday that reshaped the balance of power in Washington. In one, the justices shielded a Federal Reserve official from President Trump's firing. In the other, they gave the president unprecedented control over agencies that have operated independently for nearly a century.

First, the win for Fed independence: Lisa Cook, the first African-American woman to serve on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, will keep her job while her legal challenge plays out. The vote was 5-4, with Chief Justice John Roberts writing for the majority. Roberts argued the Fed is a "uniquely structured... entity" rooted in the tradition of the First and Second Banks of the United States. Therefore, its governors can be removed only "for cause" — neglect of duty or malfeasance — not at the president's whim.

Trump had accused Cook of falsifying documents to obtain loans on two properties she listed as primary residences. Cook vehemently denied the charges, and her lawyers accused the administration of "cherry picking" from her mortgage applications. They noted that five Trump Cabinet members, including acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, had similar applications without any suggestion of wrongdoing. The lower courts will now examine the evidence.

The Cook case is far from over, but the ruling preserves the Fed's independence — for now. No president before Trump has tried to fire a Fed board member. If Trump ultimately prevails, he could reshape the board that sets interest rates and steers the economy.

But in a separate 6-3 ruling, the Court delivered a major victory to Trump by overturning Humphrey's Executor, a 1935 precedent that protected commissioners of independent agencies like the Federal Trade Commission from at-will firing. The case involved Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, an FTC commissioner Trump fired in March 2025 without citing any cause. Roberts wrote that the president must be able to remove subordinates who exercise executive power, or else accountability to voters breaks down.

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, in dissent, called the decision "grievously wrong" and said it gives the president power "unknown even to the English Crown." The ruling effectively turns FTC commissioners into at-will employees and ends the requirement that the commission be bipartisan. The FTC enforces antitrust and consumer protection laws across 80 statutes — so the shift is seismic.

Together, the two decisions reveal a Court deeply divided on presidential power. The Fed survived this round, but the broader landscape of independent agencies has been permanently altered.
why_it_matters: These rulings affect whether agencies that oversee everything from the economy to consumer safety can be turned into political tools by the sitting president — a shift that could change what products are safe, what companies are allowed to merge, and how the government responds to financial crises for decades to come.

background_read: The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States, and its nine justices have lifetime appointments so they can make rulings without worrying about losing their jobs.

The Federal Reserve (often called 'the Fed') is the central bank of the U.S. — it sets interest rates, which affect how much it costs to borrow money for cars, homes, and businesses. Lisa Cook, the first African-American woman on its Board of Governors, is serving a 14-year term that doesn't end until 2038.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) was created by Congress in 1914 to stop unfair business practices and monopolies. For nearly a century, a 1935 Supreme Court decision called Humphrey's Executor said a president couldn't fire FTC commissioners just because he disagreed with them — they could only be removed for bad behavior or neglect.

The Constitution divides power among three branches of government — the president (executive), Congress (legislative), and the courts (judicial) — so no single person has total control. The recent cases test how far the president's power should reach into agencies that Congress designed to be somewhat independent.

perspectives.description: Supporters say that when voters elect a president, they expect that person's policies to be put in place quickly. If agency heads who disagree with the president can't be fired, the president's ability to carry out promises is weakened. This ruling ensures the executive branch is truly accountable to the public through elections.

Critics argue that agencies like the FTC were intentionally set up outside direct presidential control to make sure they enforce laws fairly, not based on who is in power. With this decision, a president could fire commissioners just for having different political views, turning regulatory bodies into partisan weapons — exactly what the founders feared.

The Court has been gradually strengthening presidential control over agencies for years. In 2020, during Trump's first term, a separate ruling allowed the president to fire the head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau without cause. The two decisions this week show a pattern: the Court is willing to treat the Fed as a special exception while dismantling the broader tradition of independent agencies built after the Great Depression.

If the rulings stand, the FTC's approach to antitrust enforcement could swing wildly with each election — heavy regulation under one president, light touch under the next. Congress may try to rewrite laws to create new protections for agency independence, but with such a narrow Supreme Court margin, further litigation is all but guaranteed.
